content.title: About
content.content: Rice crackers are light, crunchy snacks made from whole‑grain rice dough. They are typically gluten‑free, have a neutral flavor, and can be enjoyed on their own or as a base for toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice crackers are widely used in Asian cuisine as a substitute for wheat‑based breadcrumbs.
Their gluten‑free nature makes them suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.
In many countries they are served with soy sauce, wasabi, or seaweed flakes.
Some varieties are fortified with vitamins and minerals such as iron and vitamin B12.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most rice crackers contain little fat, making them appropriate for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: The absence of gluten allows inclusion in the diet of those with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Rice provides slowly released energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Their light texture and low fat content make them easy on the stomach, especially during mild gastrointestinal upset.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands are heavily salted, which can be problematic for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Low protein
items.content: Rice crackers are not a significant source of protein and should not replace protein‑rich foods.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may be allergic to rice, experiencing skin reactions or digestive issues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rice crackers can be eaten plain, spread with hummus, cream cheese, avocado, or used as a base for mini‑canapés topped with fish, vegetables, and sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Lemon is a sour citrus fruit cultivated in warm regions worldwide. It consists of juice, pulp and zest, all rich in vitamin C, flavonoids and citric acid. Raw lemon is typically eaten as wedges, zest, or grated for flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lemons were first cultivated in Southeast Asia before spreading to the Mediterranean.
Lemon juice has a pH of about 2–3, making it an excellent natural preservative.
Essential oil from lemon zest is used in perfumery, aromatherapy and cooking.
Lemon trees can live over 50 years and bear fruit nearly year‑round in suitable climates.
The acidity of lemon accelerates caramelization of sugars in cooking.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: 100 g of lemon provides roughly 53 mg of vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and citric acid help neutralize free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity stimulates gastric juice production, improving food digestion.

items.title: Helps with colds
items.content: A warm drink with lemon and honey can soothe cough and cold symptoms.

items.title: May reduce kidney stone risk
items.content: Citrate in lemon can help dissolve small stones and prevent their formation.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: The high acidity of lemon juice can wear down tooth enamel if consumed frequently without dilution.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to citrus, experiencing skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: People with ulcers or gastritis should limit intake of pure lemon juice.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Acids in lemon can affect absorption of certain drugs, such as antibiotics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lemon can be added to water, tea, salads, sauces, marinades and baked goods. Zest is used as a grated flavoring. Juice is often diluted with water to reduce acidity.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store lemons in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, wrapped in a plastic bag. At room temperature they keep 1–2 days; in the fridge up to 2 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Puerto Rican style meat loaf is a baked mixture of ground beef and pork seasoned with spices, tomato sauce, olives, and sometimes raisins. The dish has a fragrant, slightly sweet flavor with hints of garlic, onion, and paprika typical of Puerto Rican cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally it is served with rice and beans as part of a "completo" – a full Puerto Rican meal.
The recipe often uses "adobo" – a spice blend of oregano, garlic, black pepper, and dry mustard.
Meat loaf is frequently garnished with olive rings and pineapple chunks, giving it a bright visual appeal.
The dish originated in the early 20th century when American cooks adapted European meat loaf recipes to local ingredients.
Some families bake the loaf in individual muffin‑size portions rather than a single large loaf.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef and pork provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat is rich in vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: A modest amount of monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats contributes to heart‑healthy nutrition when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Paprika, garlic, and oregano provide antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: The pork component can raise saturated fat levels, which may be a concern for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Tomato sauce and added seasonings often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to oregano, garlic, or paprika.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Meat must be cooked thoroughly to avoid salmonella and other bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The loaf is usually sliced and served hot with rice, beans, fried plantains, or a fresh salad. It can also be used in sandwiches, as a taco filling, or added to soups for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the meat loaf to room temperature, then store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. For longer storage, slice and freeze portions; they keep well for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before serving.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-home-.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce (Home Recipe)

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta made from durum wheat retains the bran and germ, offering more nutrients than refined pasta. This home‑cooked version is tossed with a creamy sauce made from cream, cheese, and fresh herbs, delivering a rich and comforting flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta provides more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals than traditional white pasta.
Making the cream sauce at home lets you control salt levels and add healthy ingredients like garlic and basil.
Durum wheat, the base for most pasta, is high in protein and gluten, giving pasta its firm texture.
In Italy, whole grain pasta is called "pasta integrale" and is often paired with simple sauces to highlight its nutty taste.
Homemade cream sauce can be refrigerated for up to 3 days and frozen for up to 2 months.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta supplies dietary fiber that supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2, and B3 vitamins aid energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from the sauce
items.content: The dairy‑based cream sauce contributes calcium and vitamin D, which are essential for bone health.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: A modest amount of butter and cream provides essential fatty acids and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cream sauce contains dairy, which can cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cream sauce adds significant calories, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten and is unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Adding salt to the sauce should be monitored, especially for individuals with hypertension.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Cook the whole grain pasta in salted boiling water for 10‑12 minutes until al dente. In a separate pan melt butter, add cream, grated Parmesan, minced garlic, and fresh basil; simmer 3‑5 minutes until thickened. Toss the pasta with the sauce, adding a splash of pasta water if needed for consistency. Serve hot, garnished with extra Parmesan and herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry whole grain pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked pasta with sauce can be refrigerated for up to 2 days. Freeze in portion‑sized containers for up to 1 month after cooling.
